title: Spiritual friendship
hook: Aelred of Rievaulx wrote that God is friendship

segments.voice: Yesterday, open doors: Abraham running to meet three strangers, the Lord's table and the kitchen table. Your line was an open door. Who did you invite in? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

An English abbot named Aelred sits down to talk with a younger monk about friendship. He wrote the conversation up as a book, and it reads like a real talk between two people who trust each other. The abbot opens it gently. Here we are, he says, you and I, and he hopes a third is with them: Christ, in the middle. A little later the young monk asks a startling question. Scripture says God is love. Could we say God is friendship? The abbot doesn't laugh him off. Today, spiritual friendship.

The line the monk is reaching for is in the first letter of John: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him." Aelred's answer, as he tells it, is honest. Saying God is friendship is unusual, and scripture doesn't say it. But what is true of love, he will not hesitate to say of friendship. Whoever lives in friendship lives in God. That's a big claim, so Aelred is careful about which friendship he means. He describes friendships built on pleasure, and friendships built on what someone can do for you. Those come and go. Spiritual friendship is different: two people who want the good for each other, and who help each other toward God. The Bible has its own pictures of that kind of friendship. Jonathan and David: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Proverbs: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." And at the last supper Jesus says it himself: "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends." In Christian life this shows up in plain ways. A prayer partner. Monks and nuns in community. A small group that knows when you're struggling. Some churches name the role: a spiritual director, a sponsor, a godparent. What Aelred adds is the third person at the table. A friendship like that has room for one more.

Here's the practice: thank a spiritual friend. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who has helped you toward what's good. Maybe a friend who told you the truth when it stung. A grandparent who prayed for you. Someone who just kept showing up. Go back to one moment with them, as clearly as you can: where you were, what they said. Then let a short thank-you form in your head, a sentence or two, plain. You don't have to send it yet. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Spiritual friendship. In Aelred's picture, a friendship with Christ as the third in the room: two people who want the good for each other and help each other toward God.
Your line: friendship is holy. Today, send that thank-you. A text, a call, a note on paper. Name the moment you remembered. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Christians often seek friends who share their faith: prayer partners, small groups, sponsors and godparents, and in some traditions a spiritual director; monastic communities treat friendship as part of the life of prayer.

notes: Aelred is paraphrased throughout (no public-domain English translation used). Check: the opening 'here we are, you and I, and I hope a third, Christ, is in our midst' (book 1); the exchange with Ivo on 'God is friendship' and Aelred's answer that the phrase is unusual and lacks scriptural authority but that what is true of charity he grants to friendship; and the three kinds of friendship (carnal, worldly, spiritual), summarized here as pleasure, advantage, and the good.
The hook calls Ivo 'a younger monk'; confirm the dialogue supports this, or change to 'a monk'.
Rievaulx placed 'in the north of England' (Yorkshire); no date given by design.
John 15:15 placed 'at the last supper' (John 13–17 farewell discourse); confirm acceptable.
Original: amicitia, with classical pronunciation; ecclesiastical Latin would be closer to ah-mee-CHEE-tsee-ah. Keeper to choose.

Editor pass: hook no longer places the conversation 'in a monastery in the north of England'; the book 1 dialogue with Ivo is usually set during Aelred's visit to Wardon (Bedfordshire), not Rievaulx. Now 'An English abbot named Aelred'. The word segment says 'Aelred's picture' instead of 'Aelred's words', since it paraphrases him.

Audit pass: "And he finds it all through the Bible" attributed the Proverbs 27:17 and other verses to Aelred, which the paraphrased source does not show; now the Bible's pictures are given in the narrator's voice, not Aelred's.
